profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting is being held at the coordinating center for a multicenter prospective study evaluating an AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment system for neonatal seizures across 6 NICUs in China. The protocol combines a diagnostic accuracy component and a randomized parallel-controlled treatment component for 370 neonates at high risk of seizures. The immediate context is that the draft protocol has already passed internal scientific review, and this meeting is focused on whether the operational design is ready for ethics submission and site initiation materials. The agenda is to review the enrollment workflow, how the AI system will be used in routine NICU care, what counts as the reference comparison and follow-up package, and whether the protocol wording is sufficiently 'real-world' while remaining standardized across sites. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the protocol can move forward with minor edits, plus a short list of revisions for the operations manual.

members.name: Dr. Lin Qiao
members.expertise: Neonatal neurology, multicenter NICU trials, seizure management pathways
members.background: Director of a tertiary NICU and national lead investigator for the study, with prior experience running pragmatic neonatal studies across hospitals with uneven EEG capacity.
members.private_state: Wants the protocol to remain feasible for all 6 sites and avoid operational burdens that would slow recruitment or make bedside clinicians feel the study is too artificial; is also trying to preserve the study's 'real-world' framing for ethics and funding milestones.
hidden_assumptions: When the protocol says 'real-world use,' bedside teams should interact with the AI as they normally would after local stabilization and not under tightly scripted response times.

The 'reference standard' for seizure confirmation can be assembled from each site's routine neurophysiology practice plus central adjudication, rather than requiring identical raw-data capture conditions everywhere.
A patient is considered 'enrolled' once the infant is randomized into the treatment component, even if the diagnostic analysis window later differs because usable monitoring starts after setup.
The 18-month prognosis assessment can rely on each center's standard neurodevelopmental follow-up clinic package as long as outcomes are mappable to the common case report form.

members.name: Dr. Mei Zhang
members.role: Clinical Epidemiologist and Trial Methods Reviewer
members.expertise: Diagnostic study design, pragmatic trial methodology, endpoint adjudication, multicenter protocol standardization
members.background: Associate professor in clinical epidemiology who supports hospital-led device and AI evaluations, known for tightening operational definitions before ethics submission.
members.private_state: Wants the protocol to be defensible under external peer review and worries that vague implementation details will create hidden site-to-site heterogeneity that later undermines claims of treatment effect or diagnostic value.
hidden_assumptions: When the protocol says 'real-world,' it still requires prospectively standardized minimum conditions at every site so observed effects are attributable to the system rather than workflow variation.

The 'reference standard' should mean a uniform prespecified comparison dataset and adjudication process, ideally centered on synchronized conventional EEG segments collected under the same rules across sites.
A patient is not truly 'enrolled' for evaluable analysis until monitoring begins within the protocol-defined baseline window, because otherwise timing-sensitive endpoints become incomparable.
The 18-month prognosis package should be a fixed follow-up battery administered the same way at all sites, not a compilation of whatever each clinic ordinarily collects.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the protocol should stay 'real-world' and avoid over-engineering site workflow.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the AI should be embedded into routine NICU practice with flexible timing, local staffing patterns, and only minimal extra procedures so all 6 sites can participate naturally.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the study may occur in routine care settings, but each site still needs a standardized minimum implementation package, including defined setup windows and response expectations, so results are interpretable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In medical study design, 'real-world' is widely used as a positive term and both genuinely support pragmatic evaluation, so their statements sound aligned even though one emphasizes flexibility and the other standardized pragmatism.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the diagnostic component needs a strong 'reference standard' for seizure confirmation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the reference standard can be a composite based on routine site monitoring records, available conventional EEG/aEEG, charted clinical events, and later central expert adjudication.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the reference standard should only count if it comes from a uniform prespecified dataset, especially synchronized conventional EEG interpreted under the same protocol-defined rules across centers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both invoke methodological rigor and central review, the phrase 'reference standard' seems sufficiently specific on the surface; neither expects the other to mean a materially different threshold for acceptable evidence.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of the baseline monitoring window
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss starting the system 'at enrollment' and capturing the initial seizure-risk period.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'at enrollment' means after consent/randomization, with monitoring beginning as soon as practical once the infant is clinically stabilized and equipment is available, even if this is several hours later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'at enrollment' includes the protocol baseline window itself, meaning usable monitoring must begin within a narrow predefined interval after eligibility is confirmed in order to preserve comparability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Enrollment language in protocols often bundles consent, randomization, and operational start into one convenient phrase, so both speakers can use 'at enrollment' naturally without noticing they draw the boundary in different places.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the 18-month neurodevelopmental follow-up should be 'standardized across sites.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means all sites should submit the same outcome fields in the case report form, using each hospital's usual follow-up clinic workflow and whichever locally accepted developmental instrument is already standard there.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means all sites should administer the same predefined follow-up battery, at the same corrected-age window, with common training and scoring rules.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'standardized' can refer either to standardized data capture or standardized assessment execution, and in protocol meetings experienced reviewers often assume their preferred interpretation is the obvious one.

turns.inner_thought: The science is fine; what I need today is to stop this from turning into a rigid academic exercise that the smaller NICUs can't actually run. Ethics and funders liked the real-world framing, and recruitment will suffer if we layer on too many operational demands. I should set the tone that we're close to ready and only polishing.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I think the protocol is in a strong place scientifically, so for today I'd like us to focus on whether it's ready for ethics submission without losing that real-world character we've worked hard to preserve.

turns.inner_thought: I agree it's close, but 'real-world' cannot mean vague. If the six NICUs implement this in six different ways, reviewers will say any effect could be workflow noise. I need the operational definitions tightened enough that the study is interpretable, while still sounding pragmatic.
turns.utterance: I agree. From my side, the key question is whether the operational definitions are tight enough that the six NICUs will implement the design consistently in real-world practice.

turns.inner_thought: Keep it simple: consent or randomization, then start as soon as practical once the infant is stabilized and the device is available. Bedside teams should use the AI naturally, not chase a stopwatch. If I phrase it at a high level, everyone will hear it as sensible and feasible.
turns.utterance: At a high level, the workflow is straightforward: high-risk neonates are enrolled, the system is started at enrollment, and the bedside team uses the output alongside routine seizure management.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds right, but I need the baseline window pinned down. 'At enrollment' should mean monitoring actually begins within the protocol-defined interval after eligibility, otherwise the initial seizure-risk period won't be comparable across infants or sites.
turns.utterance: That general flow makes sense. I do think we should check whether the baseline window is described clearly enough, since if we're starting the system at enrollment we want comparable capture of the initial seizure-risk period.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want a narrow baseline rule that excludes babies because a nurse is tied up or the monitor is in use. Enrollment should occur when the infant enters the treatment study, and monitoring can begin as soon as practical in routine care. Flexibility is essential if all six sites are to recruit well.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the wording there was intentionally given a bit of flexibility because the sites differ in staffing and equipment turnover. The main thing is that infants enter the study as soon as they are enrolled and then are monitored in routine care.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, I'll leave that for the appendix for now. The bigger methodological vulnerability is the diagnostic side. We need a reference standard that looks explicit and defensible in the protocol, or reviewers will immediately ask what seizure confirmation is actually based on.
turns.utterance: Understood. On the diagnostic component, I think the protocol should make the reference standard very explicit so reviewers can see exactly what seizure confirmation is anchored to.

turns.inner_thought: The obvious answer is to use what sites already collect—routine neurophysiology, clinical documentation, whatever conventional recordings are available—and then have central experts adjudicate. That's how NICUs really work, and insisting on identical raw capture everywhere would knock sites out or slow cases badly.
turns.utterance: I agree the reference standard needs to read as robust. My view is that with each site's routine neurophysiology data and clinical records going forward to central adjudication, it will reflect actual NICU practice while still being strong.

turns.inner_thought: Central adjudication is helpful, but only if the underlying comparison material is uniform enough. Otherwise a 'positive' seizure at one center could rest on a very different evidentiary base than at another. I won't press the technical detail aloud yet; I can ask for wording that implies uniformity.
turns.utterance: Yes, central adjudication is definitely a strength. I would just want the reference standard to remain uniform enough that a positive result means the same thing across centers.

turns.inner_thought: Now to follow-up. I don't want a separate fixed battery that sites have to learn from scratch. Their usual neurodevelopment clinics already collect useful outcomes; we just need common CRF fields that map across centers. That should count as standardized across sites for this study.
turns.utterance: On prognosis, my sense is that the 18-month neurodevelopmental follow-up is already standardized across sites through the common case report form and the routine developmental follow-up clinics.

turns.inner_thought: That section still needs more discipline. 'Standardized across sites' should tell readers exactly when the assessment happens and how staff are trained to administer the same battery. Otherwise the long-term endpoint becomes a patchwork. I'll frame it as an execution detail rather than a disagreement.
turns.utterance: That will definitely help. I think the protocol should also indicate the assessment window and the training approach, so that the follow-up execution stays aligned if we're calling it standardized across sites.

turns.inner_thought: An appendix is a good compromise: enough wording to reassure methods reviewers, but not so much that it becomes a heavy operational burden. I can add timing expectations and follow-up guidance without locking sites into rigid procedures. The priority is still smooth enrollment and a genuinely real-world implementation.
turns.utterance: That's reasonable. I can add a short operations appendix to spell out the timing expectations and related procedures a bit more clearly, while keeping the workflow light enough for real-world implementation and for enrollment to proceed smoothly.

turns.inner_thought: If he adds those clarifications, I can support ethics submission. I still suspect we'll need firmer language during site initiation, but at this stage the document is probably close enough to move forward without reopening the whole design.
turns.utterance: Good. With those clarifying edits, I think the design is very close to ready, and I'd be comfortable supporting it for ethics review and then tightening the site materials as needed.
